short: The Texas Medical and Dental Schools Application Service — the single application system used by nearly all Texas medical schools, plus the state's dental and veterinary schools. Texas's version of AMCAS.
The American Medical College Application Service — the application system used by most MD schools outside Texas.
The application service used by most DO (osteopathic) schools outside Texas.
The Medical College Admission Test — a standardized exam required by medical schools, scored from 472 to 528.
Grade point average. Medical schools look at both your overall GPA and your science GPA (sometimes called BCPM: biology, chemistry, physics, math).

The Joint Admission Medical Program — a Texas program offering a supported path to guaranteed admission at a participating Texas medical school for economically disadvantaged students. You must apply during your freshman or sophomore year of college.
Your true, fixed, permanent home — the place you intend to stay, shown through things like a job, property, or family ties. Living somewhere for school alone does not establish domicile.
To actually enroll and start at a school after being accepted. Matriculant counts are smaller than acceptance counts because some accepted students go elsewhere.
The specific college courses a medical school requires you to complete before enrolling — typically biology, chemistry, and related coursework. Each school sets its own list.
Doctor of Medicine — the degree granted by allopathic medical schools. MDs and DOs both become fully licensed physicians.
Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine — the degree granted by osteopathic medical schools. DOs and MDs both become fully licensed physicians; DO training adds osteopathic manipulative medicine.
One or more years between finishing college and starting medical school. Common and not a red flag — many matriculants take at least one.
The year a student would start medical school. TMDSAS labels each application cycle by entry year — you apply during the year before your entry year.
